items.prompt: After the cart is refactored, which check still passes?
choices: getTotal() returns 40
items.length is exactly 2
items[0] is the Widget entry
items.explanation: getTotal is public behavior; the other two read storage.

items.prompt: What is the public interface of a class?
choices: Its private fields and helper functions
The order of its source lines in the file
The methods callers are meant to use
items.explanation: It is the set of methods callers rely on.

items.prompt: What is an implementation detail?
choices: Any method with an unusually long name
Internal structure free to change while behavior stays the same
The name given to the class
items.explanation: It is internal structure that outsiders must not depend on.

items.prompt: Why did 15 tests fail on the array-to-Map change?
choices: The total was calculated wrongly
They read the array directly
The Map made lookups too slow
items.explanation: They depended on storage, which was changed.

items.prompt: Did a customer see a difference after the Map change?
choices: No, nothing observable changed
Yes, the totals changed
Yes, some items disappeared
items.explanation: Every observable result was the same.

items.prompt: Which assertion tests behavior?
choices: The internal array has a length of 2
The first slot holds the Widget
The cart reports a count of 3
items.explanation: The count is what a caller can observe.

items.prompt: What does BDD stand for?
choices: Bug-driven debugging cycles
Backend data design
Behavior-driven development
items.explanation: BDD is behavior-driven development.

items.prompt: A test that reads a private field is mainly risky because...
choices: It runs noticeably too fast
It breaks when the field is refactored
It always prints too much output
items.explanation: Private layout changes without notice.

items.prompt: A discount feature renames the cart's private list from `items` to `entries`; no method changes behavior. Which test fails?
choices: One that checks `getTotal()` after two different items are added to a cart
One that checks `getItemCount()` after one Widget is added to the cart
One that asserts on the list through `cart.items`
One that builds a cart using only `addItem` calls and checks its reported total
items.explanation: Only the test touching the renamed private field fails; the others use public methods.
items.reference:
Two things a test can point at
public interface: addItem, getItemCount, getTotal
internal storage: cart.items, an array or a Map
interface checks survive a refactor
storage checks break on a refactor
Why: only the public interface is the contract; storage may change at any time.
items.learnMore:
Behavior versus implementation

A test is about behavior when the thing it checks is visible to any caller. Storage layout is visible only to the class, so a test on it fails when the layout changes even though nothing observable did.

Common mistake

Calling a test a behavior test because it has a friendly name. What it reads is what counts.
items.reflection: Think of any object you use daily. Which parts are its real interface, and which parts could be swapped without you noticing?

It expects the count to be 3 after two adds
It expects an empty cart to report 0
items.explanation: Reading a positional slot of internal storage ties the test to the list layout.

Reading fields in tests is slower than calling the cart's methods every time, and slows the suite

items.explanation: Reachable is not the same as promised. The contract is what the class intends callers to use.

items.prompt: In Given-When-Then, what does Given describe?
choices: The final result of everything
The starting situation
The action taken by the caller
items.explanation: Given sets up the situation before the action.

items.prompt: In Given-When-Then, what does Then describe?
choices: The expected observable outcome
The setup before the action
The name of the class
items.explanation: Then states what a caller can observe.

items.prompt: In Given-When-Then, what does When describe?
choices: The data at the start
The expected total value
The action performed by a caller
items.explanation: When is the action the caller takes.

items.prompt: Which Then is phrased as behavior?
choices: The internal Map has two keys
The array was sorted
getTotal() returns 40
items.explanation: A returned value is observable; the others describe storage.

items.prompt: Given-When-Then is...
choices: A new programming language for tests
A way to structure a behavior test
A test runner and reporter tool
items.explanation: It is a structure for stating a behavior.

items.prompt: For an empty cart, which Given fits?
choices: Given a cart with no items
Given an array of length zero
Given a Map with no keys
items.explanation: The empty cart is the outside view; the others name storage.

items.prompt: A Then that says 'the second slot holds Gadget' mentions...
choices: Internal layout
A public return value
Nothing at all
items.explanation: Slots are storage layout.

items.prompt: Should a When step call private helper functions?
choices: Yes, always, to save time
Only when a test is run on Fridays
No, only public actions
items.explanation: When is what a caller can do from outside.

items.prompt: Which Then keeps a Given-When-Then test about behavior?
choices: Then the internal Map holds two entries
Then the storage array is not reallocated
Then getItemCount() returns 3 for two added items
Then the private total field equals 40
items.explanation: The count is a public return value; the rest name internals.
items.reference:
Given-When-Then
Given: the starting situation
When: the caller's action
Then: what the caller can observe
no field, array or Map in any of the three
Why: it is a way to narrate a behavior test, not a different kind of test.
items.learnMore:
Given-When-Then

Each part is phrased from the outside. Given sets the scene, When is the action, Then is a result a caller can see. Nothing in the three parts should name private structure.

Common mistake

Treating Given-When-Then as a template to fill. A Then that checks a field is still an implementation test.
items.reflection: Describe a routine at home or work as given, when, then. Does the Then name something anyone could see from outside?

items.prompt: A teammate rewrites `expect(cart.items.length).toBe(2)` as Given an empty cart, When two items are added, Then items.length is 2. What is wrong?
choices: The Then still reads private storage, so only the formatting changed
Nothing is wrong, since three labelled lines make it a behavior test by definition
The Given should be a Map instead of an empty cart, so the setup matches storage
The When should call a private method directly so the action is more precise
items.explanation: Relabelling does not change what is checked.

items.prompt: An internal refactor with no behavior change should leave behavior tests...
choices: Red
Deleted
Green
items.explanation: They only depend on observable results.

items.prompt: A test that reads internal storage fails after a refactor. This is most likely...
choices: A real regression
A false alarm
A hardware fault
items.explanation: The observable behavior did not change.

items.prompt: How many behavior tests break when the array becomes a Map?
choices: None, if they use public methods
All of them, since the storage changed
Exactly half of them, at random
items.explanation: They never touched the array.

items.prompt: What does a green behavior suite guarantee?
choices: Tested behaviors are unchanged
Nothing changed anywhere
The code is fast
items.explanation: It covers only what was written down.

items.prompt: What fixes a gap in behavior coverage?
choices: Reading more private fields instead
Deleting the whole suite for now
Writing a test for the missing behavior
items.explanation: Gaps are closed with a new behavior test.

items.prompt: With 15 internals-reading tests, a storage refactor turns how many red?
items.explanation: Every one depends on storage.

items.prompt: A deliberate behavior change makes a behavior test fail. That test should be...
choices: Left red until someone notices
Updated with the change
Silenced forever with a skip flag
items.explanation: The old expectation no longer describes the intended behavior.

items.prompt: Why avoid refactors because they break tests?
choices: Often the tests are coupled to storage
Refactors are not allowed in teams
Tests cost money for every run
items.explanation: The coupling is the real problem.

items.prompt: After the Map change, 4 tests are red. Two check `getTotal()` and two check `items[0]`. What should you do?
choices: Investigate all four failures as regressions caused by the Map change
Ignore all four failures as noise, since the refactor was intended
Investigate the `getTotal()` failures; drop the storage checks
Revert the Map change at once without reading any of the failures
items.explanation: Failures on observable results may be real; failures on storage are false alarms.
items.reference:
What a green suite means
internal refactor, same behavior: stays green
observable change: goes red, correctly
untested behavior: no signal either way
red on internals only: a false alarm
Why: green means no tested behavior changed, not that nothing changed.
items.learnMore:
Reading red and green

A red test is worth investigating when it checks something a caller sees. Red on an internal-only check is a test problem. Green only covers the behaviors someone wrote down.

Common mistake

Reading a green suite as proof of no change. Untested behavior can move silently.
items.reflection: Think of a checklist you trust. What does it not check, and how would you notice a problem in that gap?

items.prompt: All behavior tests are green after a refactor, yet duplicate items now merge quantities. Which statement fits?
choices: No test covered adding the same item twice, so the change went unseen
The refactor is proven safe by the green suite
The merge change is an implementation detail and can never matter to callers
Behavior tests are structurally unable to catch any merge-related change
items.explanation: A green suite only covers behaviors that have a test.
